---
title: "Exactly-Once Business Effects from At-Least-Once Requests"
description: "High-difficulty correctness interview scenario with formal invariants and original reference code."
---

## Interview challenge

A user clicks **Pay**, the payment provider charges the card, and your HTTP response disappears. The client retries. Does a 500/timeout mean the charge failed? No. A network timeout only tells the *caller* that no timely answer arrived.

The hard task is to offer a **single business effect** even when commands are delivered multiple times. 'Exactly-once network delivery' is not necessary; a consistent idempotency contract is.

## Define the real invariant

Identify an operation by (account, idempotency key) and store a canonical request fingerprint. For a fixed identity $k$ and payload $p$, repeats should return the same committed effect:

$$
\operatorname{effect}(k,p)^n=\operatorname{effect}(k,p),\qquad n\geq1.
$$

This is idempotence of the **business effect**, not a promise that the HTTP handler runs only once. A second request with the same key but a *different* fingerprint is a conflict, not a new payment.

## Reproduce it in one tiny implementation

~~~ts
const gate = new IdempotencyGate<number>();
let charges = 0;
const action = async () => ++charges;

const a = gate.run('account7:payment8','amount=100',action);
const b = gate.run('account7:payment8','amount=100',action);
// Both resolve to 1, and charges == 1 in this process.
~~~

Run POST /lab/idempotency twice with the same key and fingerprint. The lab coalesces an in-flight Promise and retains completed results. The tests prove local deduplication and payload-conflict detection.

## The distributed version requires a transaction

An in-memory Map **does not survive restarts** or coordinate replicas. Use a database uniqueness constraint on (tenant, key) and commit the idempotency receipt with the local business mutation in the same transaction. Include states such as processing, completed, and failed/retryable, with an explicit retention policy.

The external card processor is a separate system. Use *its* idempotency capability and a stable provider operation ID, reconcile uncertain responses, and never blindly create a second charge.

## A concrete race

Two API replicas receive the same key simultaneously. Both check that it is absent. Both start a charge. This is a classic **check-then-act race**. The winning operation must be chosen by an atomic insert/uniqueness claim, not by a read followed by an unprotected write.

## Interview follow-ups

- What if the first attempt fails before any side effect? Decide whether to evict the reservation and allow retry; the lab does so for rejected Promises.
- What if the first attempt succeeds but the response body changes after deployment? Store a canonical receipt or stable result schema.
- What if a customer reuses a key six months later? Scope and retention must be part of the public contract.

## Mathematical Abstraction

$$
\forall k:\quad \bigl|\{\text{committed business effects with identity }k\}\bigr|\leq1.
$$

This at-most-one condition, combined with a guaranteed eventual completion process, is more useful than an imprecise claim that the network delivers 'exactly once'.

**Public reference:** [Microsoft Azure: Idempotent Consumer](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/azure/architecture/patterns/idempotent-consumer). The same principle applies to duplicate HTTP payments and replayed message processing.
